title: The Truth About the 1960s Kitchen Your Mother Trusted

scenes.text: Your mother's kitchen in the nineteen sixties was her pride. Gleaming appliances in harvest gold or turquoise. A spice rack. A row of canisters for flour, sugar, coffee and tea. A cabinet full of new products from the supermarket, each one promising to make her life easier, her family healthier and her house cleaner. And she trusted every one of them.
scenes.caption: THE KITCHEN SHE TRUSTED

scenes.text: Why wouldn't she? The products came from big, respected companies. They were advertised on television by friendly actors in white coats. Doctors endorsed them. Magazines praised them. In the sixties, Americans had enormous faith in science, progress and modern living.
scenes.caption: ENORMOUS FAITH

scenes.text: But some of those things turned out to be very different from what they seemed. And some of the things she was told were old-fashioned turned out to be right all along. So let's open the cupboards of the nineteen sixties kitchen, one by one, and see what we know now.
scenes.caption: WHAT WE KNOW NOW

scenes.text: Let's start under the sink. In many sixties kitchens, there was a can of bug spray, and it often contained DDT. During the fifties and early sixties, DDT was considered a miracle. It killed mosquitoes, flies and roaches. It was sprayed on crops, in homes, and even from trucks driving through neighborhoods on summer evenings.
scenes.caption: DDT

scenes.text: Kids ran behind the fogging trucks, playing in the white cloud. Nobody thought it was dangerous. Then, in nineteen sixty-two, a biologist named Rachel Carson published a book called Silent Spring. She showed that DDT was killing birds and building up in the food chain. The book caused a sensation. In nineteen seventy-two, DDT was banned in the United States for most uses.
scenes.caption: SILENT SPRING

scenes.text: Also under the sink were the cleaning products. Bleach, ammonia, scouring powder, oven cleaner and furniture polish. Mothers used them all, often in a small kitchen with the windows closed. Some even mixed bleach and ammonia, thinking two cleaners would work better than one. That mixture releases a toxic gas, and it sent many people to the hospital.
scenes.caption: UNDER THE SINK

scenes.text: And the laundry detergent of the sixties was loaded with phosphates. They made clothes whiter, but when the water went down the drain, they fed huge blooms of algae in lakes and rivers. Lake Erie became so polluted that newspapers called it dying. In the early seventies, many states banned or limited phosphates in laundry soap, and the lakes slowly recovered.
scenes.caption: PHOSPHATES

scenes.text: On the kitchen table, there might have been a little bottle of artificial sweetener. In the sixties, diet sodas became very popular, and many of them were sweetened with a chemical called cyclamate, often mixed with saccharin. Tab, Diet Rite and Fresca. Women trying to stay slim drank them by the case.
scenes.caption: DIET SODA

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty-nine, a study found that very high doses of cyclamate caused cancer in rats. The government banned it almost overnight. Companies had to reformulate their diet drinks in a hurry. Later research questioned whether cyclamate was really as dangerous as feared, and it's still allowed in many other countries. But in America, it never came back.
scenes.caption: BANNED IN 1969

scenes.text: In the cupboard, there was food coloring, and many packaged foods contained a dye called Red Dye Number Two. It was in candy, cake mixes, sausages, ice cream and soft drinks. It made maraschino cherries bright red. It was one of the most common food dyes in the country.
scenes.caption: RED DYE NUMBER TWO

scenes.text: In the seventies, studies raised concerns that Red Dye Number Two might cause cancer. In nineteen seventy-six, the government banned it. The scare was so big that the Mars company took red M and M's out of the bag for almost ten years, even though they had never used that dye. Red M and M's didn't come back until nineteen eighty-seven.
scenes.caption: RED M&Ms DISAPPEARED

scenes.text: Even the kitchen walls held a secret. Many homes built before nineteen fifty, and some built later, were painted with lead-based paint. It was durable, and it came in bright, washable colors that were perfect for a kitchen. When it chipped or peeled, small children sometimes put the flakes in their mouths, because lead tastes slightly sweet.
scenes.caption: LEAD PAINT

scenes.text: Doctors slowly learned that even small amounts of lead could harm a child's brain and development. In nineteen seventy-eight, lead paint was banned for use in homes. Leaded gasoline was phased out over the next two decades. Since then, the amount of lead in American children's blood has fallen dramatically.
scenes.caption: BANNED IN 1978

scenes.text: In the refrigerator, there was margarine. In the sixties, doctors and advertisers told Americans that butter was bad for the heart, and margarine was the healthy choice. Families switched by the millions. Crisco shortening replaced lard in pie crusts. Margarine went on toast, in cookies, and on every ear of corn.
scenes.caption: MARGARINE

scenes.text: But much of that margarine and shortening was made with partially hydrogenated oils, full of what we now call trans fats. Decades later, scientists found that trans fats were actually worse for the heart than butter. In twenty fifteen, the government ordered them removed from the food supply. Grandma's butter, it turned out, wasn't the villain.
scenes.caption: TRANS FATS

scenes.text: On the stove were the new pans. In the sixties, Teflon nonstick cookware became a sensation. Eggs slid right off. No scrubbing. Teflon was made by DuPont, and it seemed like a miracle of modern chemistry. Many women put away their heavy old cast iron skillets and bought a shiny new set.
scenes.caption: TEFLON

scenes.text: Years later, scientists raised concerns about a chemical called PFOA, which was used in making Teflon. It was found in water supplies near factories and in people's blood. By twenty fifteen, American companies had stopped using it. And many cooks went right back to the cast iron skillet their grandmothers had used all along.
scenes.caption: BACK TO CAST IRON

scenes.text: And here's a scare that went the other way. In the sixties, many kitchens had a shaker of Accent, a flavor enhancer made of monosodium glutamate, or MSG. Mothers sprinkled it on meat, soups and vegetables. Then, in nineteen sixty-eight, a doctor wrote a letter to a medical journal describing symptoms he felt after eating at Chinese restaurants.
scenes.caption: ACCENT

scenes.text: The idea spread quickly, and for decades many Americans believed that MSG was dangerous. Restaurants put up signs saying No MSG. But careful studies over many years have mostly failed to find any real harm for most people, and the FDA considers it safe. Glutamate occurs naturally in tomatoes, cheese and mushrooms. Your mother's shaker of Accent was probably fine all along.
scenes.caption: PROBABLY FINE ALL ALONG

scenes.text: In the cabinet, there were the good dishes. Many families had Fiesta ware, the brightly colored dinnerware made by the Homer Laughlin China Company in West Virginia. Red, yellow, turquoise, green and cobalt blue. It's still collected today. But the original red-orange glaze contained uranium oxide, which made it mildly radioactive.
scenes.caption: FIESTA WARE

scenes.text: For decades, families ate off those plates without knowing. Some Geiger counters still click near them today. Experts say the risk from occasional use is small, but collectors are advised not to eat from the old red pieces. Some older china and pottery also used lead in their glazes, which could leach into acidic foods like tomato sauce and orange juice.
scenes.caption: A LITTLE RADIOACTIVE

scenes.text: Even the refrigerator had a hidden danger. In the forties and fifties, refrigerators closed with a heavy latch that could only be opened from the outside. When old refrigerators were thrown out in alleys, dumps and backyards, children climbed inside to play hide-and-seek, and couldn't get out. Tragically, many children died this way.
scenes.caption: THE LATCH

scenes.text: In nineteen fifty-six, Congress passed the Refrigerator Safety Act. It required that new refrigerators could be opened from the inside. That's why refrigerator doors today close with magnets. And for years afterward, parents and teachers warned children never, ever to play in an old refrigerator.
scenes.caption: MAGNETIC DOORS

scenes.text: And in many sixties kitchens, there was an ashtray on the table. Roughly four in ten adults smoked. Mothers smoked while cooking, fathers smoked after dinner, and guests smoked over coffee. Children grew up breathing it every day. Pregnant women were often told that a few cigarettes were fine, even relaxing.
scenes.caption: THE ASHTRAY ON THE TABLE

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty-four, the Surgeon General's report linked smoking to lung cancer. Warning labels appeared on packs in nineteen sixty-six. Cigarette ads were banned from television in nineteen seventy-one. Over the next decades, millions of parents quit, often because their children begged them to.
scenes.caption: 1964: THE WARNING

scenes.text: But here's the other side of the story. A lot of what your mother did in that kitchen turned out to be exactly right. She cooked from scratch. She used fresh vegetables from the garden or the market. She made soup from leftovers, and wasted almost nothing. Today, nutrition experts tell us to do exactly that.
scenes.caption: FROM SCRATCH

scenes.text: She served smaller portions. A sixties dinner plate was about nine or ten inches wide. Today, many dinner plates are eleven or twelve inches. A soft drink came in a little six-and-a-half-ounce glass bottle. A candy bar was smaller. Families ate snacks less often, and dessert was a treat, not a habit.
scenes.caption: SMALLER PLATES

scenes.text: She also canned and preserved. Tomatoes, green beans, jams and pickles, put up in glass jars every summer. It was a lot of work, but she knew exactly what was in every jar. Today, home canning has come back into fashion, and many young families are rediscovering the skills that their grandmothers took for granted.
scenes.caption: SHE KNEW WHAT WAS IN EVERY JAR

scenes.text: She used cast iron and glass. Pyrex baking dishes and Corning Ware, which went from the freezer to the oven to the table. Those dishes last for generations, and many families still use their mothers' casserole dishes today. Some of those patterns, like Spring Blossom and Butterprint, are now treasured collectibles.
scenes.caption: PYREX AND CORNING WARE

scenes.text: And she didn't waste anything. Bacon grease was saved in a can by the stove for frying. Stale bread became bread pudding or stuffing. Chicken bones became broth. Old clothes became dish rags. The idea that you should reduce, reuse and recycle was something she practiced every day, long before anyone made a slogan out of it.
scenes.caption: SHE WASTED NOTHING

scenes.text: And she sat the whole family down at the table, every night. Researchers today have found that children who eat regular family dinners tend to do better in school, eat healthier, and have fewer problems as teenagers. Your mother didn't need a study to tell her that. She just knew.
scenes.caption: SHE JUST KNEW

scenes.text: So what's the lesson of the sixties kitchen? It's not that our mothers were foolish. They trusted the experts, the scientists, the doctors and the companies, just like most people do today. Some of what the experts said turned out to be wrong. And some of what grandma did turned out to be right.
scenes.caption: THEY TRUSTED THE EXPERTS

scenes.text: Maybe in fifty years, people will look back at our kitchens and wonder what we were thinking. The things we trust today might be the stories our grandchildren tell. That's the way it always goes.
scenes.caption: IN FIFTY YEARS

scenes.text: But whatever was in those cupboards, what most of us remember about our mothers' kitchens isn't the chemicals. It's the smell of pot roast on Sunday. The sound of the mixer. Licking the beaters. And the feeling of being at home, with someone who loved you, making dinner.
scenes.caption: LICKING THE BEATERS

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What was in your mother's kitchen that would never be allowed today? And what did she do that you still do now? We read every comment. Next time, we're going to the suburbs of nineteen fifty-eight, and finding out why everyone left the city. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT WAS IN HER KITCHEN?
